source: TBJUSD All State and Local Indicators workbook (from the adopted LCAP)

rows.baseline: 92.3% of TBJUSD are credentialed for the classes they are teaching.
rows.insight: Credentialing remained flat at 92.3% across all three reporting points and did not move toward the 100% target. For the next cycle, this is a persistent capacity issue to monitor alongside recruitment, assignment, induction, and retention data so the district can distinguish vacancies, authorizations, and hard-to-staff subjects.

rows.baseline: 100% of students have access to standards-aligned instructional materials.
rows.insight: Access was maintained at 100% throughout the cycle and met the target. For the next cycle, this metric is best treated as a maintenance measure, with attention to whether newly adopted or supplemental materials remain aligned and accessible to all students.

rows.baseline: Most standards areas were rated 3/5 (Initial Development); History-Social Science and World Language were 2/5 (Beginning Development).
rows.y1: Most areas remained 3/5; History-Social Science and World Language increased to 3/5.
rows.y2: Most areas remained 3/5; NGSS decreased to 2/5; History-Social Science and World Language remained 3/5.
rows.diff: Decrease in one area; no increase
rows.insight: Implementation showed limited systemwide movement: two areas improved from 2 to 3, but most remained at 3 and NGSS declined from 3 to 2. For the next cycle, consider fewer, clearly defined implementation milestones by content area, especially NGSS, with evidence of professional learning, materials, classroom use, and follow-through.

rows.baseline: 74.3 points below standard (Red). EL, Hispanic, SED, and SWD were identified in Red in the baseline data.
rows.y1: 48.8 points below standard (Yellow); several groups improved, while LTELs remained Red.
rows.y2: 68.4 points below standard (Orange). EL, Hispanic, LTEL, and SED were Red; White was Orange.
rows.target: Increase to at least 70 points below standard or better.
rows.insight: ELA is better than the baseline but lost much of the Year 1 gain, and multiple student groups were Red in Year 2. For the next cycle, the district has a strong reason to center subgroup-specific ELA needs, especially EL/LTEL, Hispanic, and SED students, and to use interim measures that can show whether interventions are changing performance before the annual Dashboard result.

rows.baseline: 113.7 points below standard (Red). EL, Hispanic, SED, and SWD were identified in Red in the baseline data.
rows.y2: 110.2 points below standard; EL, Hispanic, LTEL, and SED were Red; White was Orange.
rows.target: Increase to at least 95 points below standard or better.
rows.insight: Math improved in Year 1 but nearly returned to the baseline level in Year 2, with pronounced gaps for EL/LTEL, Hispanic, and SED students. For the next cycle, math should remain a priority outcome with shorter-cycle diagnostics tied to specific instructional responses and student-group monitoring.

rows.metric: 4e Rate of EL students making progress toward English proficiency
rows.insight: EL progress improved over baseline at all three reporting levels, but Year 2 declined from Year 1 and THS remained below its 35% target. For the next cycle, preserve the gains while examining why progress is less stable at THS and for long-term English learners.

rows.baseline: TBJ 12.9%; TBES 4.6%; THS 24.1%. LTEL 6+ years: 22.1%.
rows.target: TBJ 20%; TBES 10%; THS 30%; reduce LTEL 6+ years to 11.6%.
rows.insight: Reclassification rates increased substantially above baseline and exceed the listed site/district targets. For the next cycle, sustain reclassification while adding post-reclassification monitoring so higher reclassification rates are paired with continued academic access and success.

rows.baseline: TBJUSD does not offer AP courses.
rows.y1: TBJUSD does not offer AP courses.
rows.y2: TBJUSD does not offer AP courses.
rows.target: TBJUSD does not offer AP courses.
rows.insight: AP is not an available pathway in the current program, so this metric does not show progress. For the next cycle, the district can continue documenting non-applicability while using other college-readiness pathways such as dual enrollment, CTE, and A–G completion to evaluate access to advanced coursework.

rows.baseline: Winter 2024: Math 5% at/above 80th percentile; ELA/Reading 2%.
rows.y2: Math: Fall 2025 29%; Winter 2026 33%. ELA/Reading: Fall 2025 25%; Winter 2026 35%.
rows.diff: Math +28; ELA/Reading +33 percentage points (winter vs. baseline)
rows.insight: Local NWEA outcomes increased substantially and exceeded the stated 20% targets, even while state ELA/math results were less stable. For the next cycle, this divergence is important to study: align local assessment windows, standards, and student groups with state results so local growth can be interpreted as evidence of readiness for CAASPP performance.

rows.baseline: Professional learning 3/5; aligned materials 2/5; staff support to identify instructional improvement areas 2/5.
rows.y1: Professional learning 3/5; aligned materials 2/5; staff support 3/5.
rows.y2: Professional learning 3/5; aligned materials 4/5; staff support 3/5.
rows.diff: Increase in one area; no decrease
rows.insight: The strongest movement was in aligned instructional materials, which increased from 2/5 to 4/5. Professional learning stayed at 3/5 and staff support rose to 3/5 then held. For the next cycle, the planning opportunity is to convert improved materials access into consistent instructional implementation, with explicit evidence of teacher practice and EL access to grade-level content.

rows.baseline: 2022–23: TBES 19.23% met/exceeded; THS 9.09%; district 12.35%.
rows.insight: Science rose in Year 1 but fell below baseline in Year 2 at both sites and districtwide. For the next cycle, this pattern supports a closer look at science standards implementation, instructional time, curriculum/materials, and site-level performance because the Priority 2 NGSS implementation rating also declined.

A–G completion declined substantially across the cycle and is far from the 70% target. For the next cycle, this warrants a focused analysis of course access, successful completion, scheduling, counseling, credit recovery, and which student groups are falling off the A–G pathway.

CTE pathway completion moved from 0% to 25% by Year 2, indicating meaningful movement but still halfway to the 50% target. For the next cycle, sustain the expanded pathway work and monitor pathway enrollment, persistence, and completion by student group so access translates into completed pathways.

rows.metric: 4b A-G completion and CTE pathway completion rate
rows.insight: Completion of both A–G and CTE increased from 0% to 8.3%, but remains well below the 50% target. For the next cycle, monitor whether students can complete both pathways without schedule conflicts and whether counseling/course sequencing makes the combined outcome realistically attainable.

rows.baseline: THS ELA 88.9 points below standard (Red); THS Math 163.9 points below standard (Red).
rows.target: ELA at least 70 below; Math at least 95 below.
rows.diff: ELA +19 points; Math +16 points vs. baseline
rows.insight: Both ELA and math remain better than baseline but worsened from Year 1; math remains far from the target and both returned to Red in Year 2. For the next cycle, use this as a bridge metric between high-school coursework and postsecondary readiness, with course-level analysis of where students lose readiness.

rows.baseline: 2023 CCI: 26.1% prepared.
rows.insight: CCI fell sharply in Year 1 and partially recovered in Year 2, but remains below baseline and far from the 50% target. For the next cycle, connect CCI planning directly to its component pathways—A–G, CTE, dual enrollment, and other qualifying measures—so the district can see which components are producing prepared graduates and where gaps remain.

rows.metric: 7a.b.c Access to and enrollment in a Broad Course of Study
rows.baseline: 100% access; courses included Computer Science, Multimedia, English, Spanish, Health, Math, PE, Science, History/Social Science, Agriculture/CTE, and AVID.
rows.y2: 100% access; offerings expanded to include Yearbook, World Language, Work Study, and Fine Arts.
rows.insight: Access remained at 100% and the listed course offerings expanded by Year 2. For the next cycle, maintain universal access while adding enrollment and successful-completion data by student group, because access alone does not show whether students are equitably participating in the full range of courses.

rows.baseline: Priority 3 self-reflection included mostly ratings of 2–4; IEP meeting attendance: 46 meetings.
rows.y1: Self-reflection remained largely 2–4; IEP meeting attendance: 56 meetings.
rows.y2: Self-reflection remained largely 3–4; IEP meeting attendance: 54 meetings.
rows.target: Move practices toward 4/5 Full Implementation; maintain IEP meeting opportunities.
rows.insight: Family engagement shows some progress but not uniform movement. IEP meeting participation increased from 46 to 54 meetings, while several self-reflection practices remained at Initial Implementation and one welcoming-environment rating declined from 4 to 3. For the next cycle, identify a small set of engagement practices that can be measured consistently and disaggregated by underrepresented family groups.

The middle school dropout rate remained at 0% throughout the cycle. For the next cycle, maintain this outcome and use early-warning indicators such as attendance, course failure, and engagement to detect risk before dropout occurs.

The high school dropout rate returned to 0% after a sharp Year 1 increase to 9.7%. For the next cycle, the volatility itself is important: track individual early-warning factors and cohort context so the district can determine whether the Year 1 spike reflected a concentrated group of students or a broader system issue.

Graduation fell sharply in Year 1 and then recovered above baseline to 97.2%. For the next cycle, the district should preserve the recovery while examining the factors behind year-to-year volatility and monitoring credit accumulation and graduation status earlier than senior year.

rows.baseline: 2023: 4% all students.
rows.insight: Suspension declined from 4.0% to 1.4%, exceeding the stated 3% target. For the next cycle, sustain the overall reduction and disaggregate by student group because the LCAP identifies White students as Red for suspension in the 2024–25 Dashboard context.

Expulsions remained at 0% across the cycle. For the next cycle, maintain this outcome while continuing to monitor exclusionary discipline and alternative responses so low expulsion does not mask inequities in suspensions or other removals.

rows.metric: 6c Pupils, parents, and teachers on sense of safety and school connectedness
rows.baseline: Kelvin Pulse favorable: Grades 4–6 66%; 7–8 60%; 9–12 64%.
rows.insight: Student climate results improved in every grade span and exceeded the 75% target in Year 2. For the next cycle, sustain the favorable trend while checking whether the gains are consistent by site and student group and whether parent/teacher climate data are also collected as described by the metric.

rows.baseline: In Good Repair
rows.insight: Facilities remained in good repair for all three reporting points. For the next cycle, continue this as a maintenance indicator and pair it with timely response to site/classroom facility needs so emerging deficiencies are visible before they affect learning conditions.

rows.diff: THS +1.41; TBES +1.37 percentage points vs. baseline
rows.insight: Attendance improved relative to the district baseline, with both sites near 94% in Year 2. Because the baseline is districtwide while annual outcomes are site-level, the next cycle should use a consistent level of reporting and include student-group attendance to show where remaining attendance gaps are concentrated.

rows.baseline: 2023: 43.2% chronically absent.
rows.insight: Chronic absenteeism declined by 22.8 percentage points and is within 0.4 points of the target. For the next cycle, sustain the overall reduction while disaggregating by student group and site so the district can identify which students remain chronically absent and whether improvement is equitable.

1.pattern: Two maintenance measures are stable; credentialing is persistently below target.
1.progress: Instructional materials stayed at 100%; facilities stayed in good repair.
1.need: Appropriately credentialed teachers remained 92.3% for all three reporting points.
1.equity: Which subjects, grades, or student groups are most affected by vacancies, misassignments, permits, or non-full credentials?
1.direction: Separate staffing capacity measures from basic-services maintenance measures; track recruitment, assignment, and retention more precisely.

2.pattern: Standards implementation is mostly stalled at Initial Implementation, with a decline in NGSS; EL materials improved.
2.need: Most standards areas remain 3/5; NGSS fell to 2/5.
2.equity: Where do EL/LTEL students experience the largest gap between available materials and enacted grade-level instruction?
2.direction: Use fewer implementation milestones with observable evidence of practice, especially for NGSS and ELD.

3.pattern: Family engagement shows modest progress but several measures remain combined or qualitative.
3.progress: IEP meeting attendance ended above baseline; some self-reflection areas moved from 2 to 3.
3.need: Several practices remain at Initial Implementation, and separate measures for unduplicated families are not reported.
3.equity: Which families participate least often, and what barriers are reported by EL, low-income, Foster Youth, and SWD families?
3.direction: Add disaggregated participation/experience measures and connect them to specific engagement practices.

4.pattern: Academic and college-readiness results are mixed, with some strong EL reclassification growth but persistent ELA/math and A–G concerns.
4.progress: EL reclassification increased sharply; CTE completion rose to 25%.
4.need: ELA/math remain weak for several student groups; A–G fell to 22.2%; science fell below baseline; EAP math remains far below target.
4.equity: Which instructional, course-taking, and student-group patterns explain the difference between strong local NWEA growth and weaker state outcomes?
4.direction: Center ELA/math subgroup gaps, science implementation, and coherent secondary pathway monitoring in the next needs assessment.

5.pattern: Attendance and chronic absenteeism improved substantially; graduation/dropout results show year-to-year volatility.
5.progress: Chronic absenteeism dropped from 43.2% to 20.4%; attendance approached 94% at both sites.
5.need: High school dropout and graduation shifted sharply in Year 1 before recovering.
5.equity: Which student groups and individual attendance patterns remain concentrated among chronically absent students?
5.direction: Maintain successful attendance systems while adding student-group and early-warning measures for persistence and graduation.

6.pattern: Overall discipline and climate trends are strong, but subgroup discipline should remain visible.
6.progress: Suspension fell to 1.4%; expulsions stayed at 0%; climate favorable ratings exceeded 75% in all grade spans.
6.need: The LCAP notes White students were Red for suspension in the 2024–25 Dashboard context.
6.equity: Are climate and discipline gains shared across student groups, sites, and grade spans?
6.direction: Keep overall measures but add subgroup/site views so favorable averages do not obscure disparities.

7.pattern: Universal course access was maintained and offerings expanded, but participation/completion equity is not visible.
7.progress: 100% access across all three years with additional course offerings in Year 2.
7.need: Combined 7a.b.c reporting does not separately show participation for unduplicated students or SWD.
7.equity: Who enrolls in and successfully completes CTE, A–G, dual enrollment, work study, and fine arts?
7.direction: Move from access-only reporting to access + participation + completion by student group.

8.pattern: Local NWEA outcomes improved strongly, while CCI remains below baseline and target.
8.progress: NWEA Math and ELA/Reading exceeded the stated 20% target.
8.need: CCI is 20.6% prepared versus 26.1% baseline and 50% target.
8.equity: How well do local assessment gains predict state assessment and postsecondary readiness outcomes for each student group?
8.direction: Use a coherent outcome set that connects local academic growth to CCI components and state performance.
